objective: Investigate an apparent early-arrival anomaly in a long-baseline neutrino time-of-flight measurement.

observations.observation: A long-baseline experiment reports neutrino events arriving about 60 nanoseconds earlier than expected from the measured source-to-detector baseline and the speed of light.
The apparent effect corresponds to a very small fractional timing difference but would have major theoretical implications if genuine.
The result is based on synchronization between a source facility and a distant detector using GPS-linked timing equipment.
The measurement requires accurate determination of proton extraction time, detector timestamps, baseline distance, and clock synchronization.
Independent measurements at the same distant laboratory using other detector systems report neutrino time-of-flight results consistent with the speed of light.
Short-pulsed source measurements can provide a more precise association between the emitted particle beam and the detected events.

constraints: Do not assume faster-than-light propagation is the cause.
Investigate the complete timing and synchronization chain.
Give independent contradictory measurements substantial weight.
Distinguish a measurement anomaly from a new physical phenomenon.
Propose a test that can distinguish instrumentation error from genuine propagation physics.
